name: Seville
info: Seville is a city on the lower Guadalquivir in south-western Spain, founded in the 8th century BCE or earlier as a Tartessian settlement, later the Roman Hispalis, a taifa capital, an Almohad capital and the port of the Spanish Empire's American trade.

facts.founded: Its original core dates to the 8th century BCE, when the town stood on an island in the Guadalquivir. By myth Hercules, identified with the Phoenician god Melqart, founded it; the Tartessians called it Spal or Ispal, and the Romans Latinised the name as Hispalis.
facts.where: On the lower reaches of the River Guadalquivir in the south-west of the Iberian Peninsula, about 80 km from the Atlantic, in Andalusia, Spain.
facts.known: Roman Hispalis; the Visigothic bishops Leander and Isidore; the capital of the Abbadid taifa; Almohad capital with the Giralda and the Torre del Oro; the Casa de Contratación and the monopoly of the American trade; the plague of 1649; the painters Velázquez, Murillo and Zurbarán; the Ibero-American Exposition of 1929 and Expo '92
facts.today: Seville is the capital of the autonomous community of Andalusia and of the province of Seville, and the fifth-largest city of Spain.

t: Seville grew from a Tartessian settlement into the Roman city of Hispalis, a Visigothic royal residence at times, the seat of al-Andalus until 716, the capital of the Abbadid taifa from 1023 and a twin capital of the Almohad empire from 1163.

Ferdinand III took it after a siege of fifteen months in 1248, and from 1503 its port held the monopoly of trade with the Spanish Americas, which brought it to more than a hundred thousand people in the 16th century.
Silting of the Guadalquivir and the plague of 1649 began a decline, the Casa de Contratación went to Cádiz in 1717, and the city later hosted the Ibero-American Exposition of 1929 and Expo '92.
dyk: Seville's motto NO8DO is a rebus read as the Spanish "No me ha dejado", "She has not abandoned me", with a figure eight standing for madeja, a skein of wool; according to legend Alfonso X gave it to the city after its people stayed loyal to him against his son.

sections.origins:
Seville stands on the lower Guadalquivir in the south-west of the Iberian Peninsula, in a fertile valley where the average height above sea level is 7 metres. The original core of the town, in the neighbourhood of the present Cuesta del Rosario, dates to the 8th century BCE, when it stood on an island in the river. Excavations in 1999 found human remains under the north wall of the Real Alcázar dating to the 8th or 7th century BCE. The town was called Spal or Ispal by the Tartessians, the pre-Roman people who controlled the Guadalquivir valley and traded with the neighbouring Phoenician colonies on the coast. The name Hisbaal is also recorded, and one proposal links it to the god Baal.

By myth the founder was Hercules, commonly identified with the Phoenician god Melqart, who was said to have sailed through the Strait of Gibraltar and founded trading posts at the sites of Cádiz and Seville. One derivation takes the name Sevilla from the Phoenician word for "lowland" or "plain". The Carthaginians gained dominance in the western Mediterranean in the 6th century BCE, and later Greek sources blamed their assaults for the destruction of Tartessos, which had collapsed by 530 BCE, either by armed conflict or by the cutting off of Greek trade. The Tartessians were succeeded by the Turdetani and the Turduli.
sections.growth:
Under Rome the city was Hispalis. It developed into one of the great market and industrial centres of Hispania, while the nearby Italica, founded in 206 or 205 BCE and the birthplace of the emperors Trajan and Hadrian, remained a residential city. Hispalis had walls and a forum, and was a commercial port on the river the Romans called the Baetis. The poet Ausonius ranked it tenth among the most important cities of the empire. Under Muslim rule it was reportedly depopulated for a time after the capital of al-Andalus moved briefly to Córdoba in 1162. After Seville became the Almohads' seat in 1163 a large urban renewal followed, and by the end of the 12th century the walled city perhaps held 80,000 people. The Giralda was raised between 1184 and 1198 and the Torre del Oro built around 1200.

The greatest age came after 1503, when the Casa de Contratación made Seville the gateway of the Indies. As the only port with the royal monopoly of trade with the Spanish Americas, it drew merchants from across Europe, who had to come to Seville for American goods. Its factories in Triana made soap, silk and ceramics, and the population grew to more than a hundred thousand, making it the largest and most urbanised city in Spain at the time. The Royal Mint of 1585 to 1587 turned American gold and silver into coin.
sections.rulers:
Visigoths held Hispalis from the 5th century after the Vandals under Gunderic in 426 and the Suebi under Rechila in 441, and the royal residence was moved there under Amalaric, Theudis and Theudigisel before it was fixed at Toledo. In 585 the king's son Hermenegild, newly converted to Catholicism, rebelled in the city against his father Leuvigild and was executed. Seville was taken for the Umayyad Caliphate in 712 or 713, and the governor of al-Andalus sat there until 716, when the capital moved to Córdoba. After the fall of the Caliphate of Córdoba an independent taifa under the Abbadid dynasty was based in Seville from 1023 until the Almoravids conquered it in 1091. The Almohads took it in the mid-12th century, and in 1163 it became the definitive seat of their Andalusi lands, alongside Marrakesh.

Ferdinand III of Castile laid siege to the city in 1247 and it surrendered on 23 November 1248. He died in the Alcázar in 1252 and was buried in the cathedral. His son Alfonso X kept Seville as one of the kingdom's capitals, and the court, which had no permanent seat, most often resided there. The Catholic Monarchs placed the Casa de Contratación in the city in 1503, and the new Bourbon administration moved it to Cádiz in 1717. The Spanish Inquisition held its first tribunal at Seville in 1478.
sections.life:
Under Umayyad rule most of the population were Muladi converts to Islam, with Christian and Jewish minorities, and the city remained the see of a Metropolitan Archbishop until the Almohads arrived in the 12th century. The Ibn Adabbas Mosque, built in 830 as the main congregational mosque, later became the Church of San Salvador. In the taifa period Seville was an important scholarly and literary centre. After the Castilian conquest churches were built in the Mudéjar and Gothic styles, and the cathedral rose on the site of the great mosque, begun after 1401 and finished in 1506. Alfonso X founded general schools of Arabic and Latin in 1254, and the present University of Seville dates its foundation to 1505.

In the 16th century the city had consulates of European governments and merchants from across the continent, and the Casa de Contratación trained pilots and taught cosmography and mathematics. The Seville of Cervantes, who lived there between 1596 and 1600, is the setting of his Rinconete y Cortadillo. In the 17th century the city became one of convents, with 45 monasteries and 28 convents for women by 1671. Murillo, Zurbarán, Valdés Leal and the sculptor Martínez Montañés worked there, and Velázquez was born in the city. The Holy Week processions, organised by lay brotherhoods, took their form in the same period. Seville's first newspaper outside Madrid appeared in 1758.
sections.crises:
Vikings sailed up the Guadalquivir in 844 and took Seville by storm. They inflicted many casualties and took hostages for ransom, and the emir of Córdoba, Abd ar-Rahman II, met them in a battle at Tablada, where about a thousand Vikings fell and four hundred were captured and executed. In the 14th century the Black Death of 1348 and an earthquake in 1356 struck the city, and in 1391 it was the starting point of anti-Jewish massacres that spread across Castile and Aragon. About 4,000 Jews were killed, many others were forced to convert, all the synagogues were seized and made into churches, and the Jewish quarter virtually disappeared. The first auto de fe of the Inquisition took place in Seville on 6 February 1481, when six people were burned alive.

In the 17th century silting of the Guadalquivir made the port harder to use, and the great plague of 1649, worsened by flooding, may have killed some 60,000 of about 130,000 people. The population did not recover until the early 19th century. Yellow fever in 1800 wiped out a third of the population, and French troops under Marshal Victor occupied the city from February 1810 until 27 August 1812. At the start of the Civil War General Queipo de Llano took the city in July 1936, resistance in the working-class quarters was crushed, and repression until January 1937 killed 3,028 people. A flood of the Tamarguillo in November 1961 inundated whole neighbourhoods.
sections.legacy:
The Alcázar, the cathedral and the General Archive of the Indies form a UNESCO World Heritage Site in the old town. The Alcázar began in the 10th century as a governor's palace, was enlarged under the Abbadids and rebuilt in Mudéjar style under Pedro I in the 1360s. The cathedral incorporates the minaret of the Almohad mosque as its bell tower, the Giralda, raised to about 95 metres by a Renaissance belfry. The Archive, designed by Juan Herrera in 1572 for the merchants' guild, became the archive of the Indies in 1785 and holds documents on the Spanish Empire in the Americas and the Philippines. The Royal Tobacco Factory, built between 1728 and 1771, is now the seat of the university's rectorate.

The Ibero-American Exposition of 1929 left the María Luisa Park and the Plaza de España, and Expo '92 left a technology park on the island of La Cartuja. The city is also known for its operas: a study of 2012 counted 153 set there, among them Mozart's The Marriage of Figaro, Rossini's The Barber of Seville and Bizet's Carmen. Seville is today the capital of Andalusia, with a municipal population of about 688,714 and a river port that is the only one in Spain.

summary: Seville, on the lower Guadalquivir in south-western Spain, grew from a Tartessian settlement into Roman Hispalis, an Abbadid and Almohad capital and, after 1503, the port of the Spanish Empire's American trade. Silting and plague ended its monopoly, and it is now the capital of Andalusia.
notes: START: the articles date the original core to the 8th century BCE (island in the Guadalquivir) and remains under the Alcázar to the 8th-7th century BCE; I used -750 with circa true. The main article also says Seville is 'approximately 2,200 years old' (Roman), which I did not use.

CONQUEST OF 712/713: the main article says Musa took it seemingly in the late summer of 712 and Abd al-Aziz retook it in July 713; the history article says Abd al-Aziz took it in 712 after a long siege. I wrote '712 or 713' in the rulers section and gave 712 in the key events and takeaways.

VIKINGS 844: both give 844 but differ on the day (main: arrived by 25 September, fell 1 October, held 40 days; history: arrived 1 October, took the city by storm on 3 October, battle at Tablada 11 November). I give 844 and the Tablada figures only (about a thousand casualties, 400 captured and executed).

ALMOHAD CONQUEST: the main article says 17 January 1147; the history article says 1149. I left the year out and wrote 'mid-12th century'. The main article's 80,000 inhabitants is hedged 'perhaps' and kept so.

GIRALDA: the history article gives the minaret as built 1184-1198; the main article calls it the Almohad minaret and gives the Renaissance belfry total height as 'around 95 or 96 metres'; I wrote about 95 metres. The main article says the Torre del Oro dates to 1220-1221, the history article says built around 1200: I wrote 'around 1200' in growth and did not repeat the date elsewhere (disputed).

WALLS: the main article says Caesar's walls were first built in ancient times; the history article also says the walls and forum were built in 45 BC after Munda, and gives the colony date confusingly ('49 BC, five years before ... 54 BC'). I left out Caesar's colony status and the walls' dates.
ROMAN TENTH PLACE: the history article says Ausonius ranked Hispalis tenth among the cities of the empire; kept.

PLAGUE OF 1649: the history article says 'may have killed some 60,000 people, nearly half of the existing population of 130,000'; the main article says 'almost half'. I kept the hedged figure. The history article also says the population was 'halved'; the event label says 'halves' - the editor may prefer 'nearly halves'.

CASA DE CONTRATACIÓN TRANSFER: the main article says control of the Casa went to Cádiz in 1717 and of the fleets in 1680; the history article says 1717 for the Casa and that Charles IV abolished it in 1790 (not used). Silting 'in the 1620s' (main) not used; I wrote only that the Guadalquivir silted in the 17th century (history: 'gradually silting in').

POPULATION: 'more than a hundred thousand' is given for the 16th century by both articles. The article says Seville's population on the present is 688,714 'as of 2025'; I wrote about 688,714 without the year, as the guide asks.
EVENT 'Seville is taken ... 712': the main article says 'seemingly' taken in 712 and retaken 713. Wording for the events section may need softening.

LEFT OUT: the 1478 Inquisition tribunal is in rulers only; the 1502 forced conversion of Muslims, Black residents (three per cent in the 16th century), the Lisbon earthquake of 1755, the 1941 Santa Bárbara explosion, 1810 occupation details beyond the dates, democratic-era politics, ETA attacks, tourism, sport, climate, transport, economy and 'In popular culture' sections (outside a history). The 'Notable people' list is not used.

The article says Fernando III's conquest terms contemplated eviction of the population and 'contemporary sources seemingly confirm' a mass movement out of Seville; I did not include this because of the hedge, though the editor may want it in crises or rulers.

UNIVERSITY: the main article says the University of Seville was founded in 1505; the history article says Alfonso X's 1254 foundation did not continue and the present university's foundation is 1505. I wrote both as the history article states.
